Welcome to the reading list, a weekly roundup of news and links related to buildings, infrastructure, and industrial technology. This week we look at Icon’s fundraising, employment in China’s solar industry, grid-scale battery reliability, Tesla’s flying roadster, and more. Roughly 2/3rds of the reading list is paywalled, so for full access become a paid subscriber.

Housekeeping items this week:

I was on MTS Live talking about robots, prefabricated construction, and other things.

I’m quoted in this Dispatch article about data center construction.

Housing and Cities

From the annals of “ suspicious discontinuities,” New York City has a tax break for new projects that set aside some proportion of the units as affordable housing called “485-x.” If a project has more than 99 units, the required share of units that are “affordable” goes up, and so do the wages that need to be paid for construction workers, resulting in a very large number of projects that are exactly 99 units. [ X ] [ Housing Wire ]

DR Horton, the largest homebuilder in the US, signed an agreement to access the services of Canadian construction automation startup Promise Robotics for more than 1250 homes. Promise seems to offer some sort of AI-driven, robotic factory-based construction service. “ Promise Robotics applies AI across the homebuilding production process by interpreting existing home designs, generating production plans and robotic instructions, orchestrating manufacturing, and connecting that production with site installation.” [ Promise Robotics ] One possible future I see for construction automation is “AI + robotics changes the logic of prefab construction and makes it more attractive,” so it’ll be interesting to see if things like this play out.

Also in construction automation news, construction 3D printing startup Icon raises a $200 million series D, at a $1.4 billion valuation. [ Dealroom ] This is surprising to me: I had sort of assumed things weren’t going well for the company. Though this does seem to be a “down round” — in 2022 its valuation was supposedly “ approaching $ 2 billion ” — I’m nevertheless adjusting my probabilities of success for Icon upward somewhat.

Some interesting data from Harvard’s Joint Center for Housing Studies on immigrants in the US construction industry. One stat I found notable: between 2013 and 2024, the number of foreign-born workers who were construction laborers or carpenters increased massively, even as the number of native-born workers in those occupations declined. But for electricians and plumbers (licensed professions), most of the increase came from native-born workers. [ Harvard JCHS ]

Manufacturing

GlobalFoundries, the semiconductor manufacturer that was spun off from AMD in 2009, will operate two new fabs planned for New York, funded by $21 billion from Japan. The US government is also taking a 4% equity stake in the company. [ GlobalFoundries ]

ASML says it can’t currently meet customer demand for lithography machines for 2027 and 2028, and is looking for ways to increase capacity. [ ASML ]

Ruthless competition in China’s solar industry: employment at China’s five biggest solar manufacturers fell 21% last year, and 31% the year before. [ Reuters ]

The US isn’t the only country with a small number of companies that make the grain-oriented electrical steel (GOES) needed for power transformers. Only two EU companies, Thyssenkrupp and Stalprodukt, make it, and as in the US they can’t make the highest quality steel. “ The global leaders—the companies that make the world’s best GOES—by and large are in [South] Korea and Japan,” Alimento says. “In the U.S. and in the EU, domestic manufacturers are not capable of making that quality of GOES, because it is a heavily protected trade secret. ” [ IEEE Spectrum ]

Thanks to ongoing memory shortages as a result of AI data center construction, smartphone shipments are down 20% year over year. [ Counterpoint ]

item.title: A Learning a Day: Hermit mode
item.description:
I’ve been thinking about an approach to the internet I’ve been calling hermit mode.

Social media was never a big habit for me, so cutting that wasn’t much of a difference. But I used to spend real time catching up on news, soccer especially, which has always been a weak spot for me. Over time, I pared general news down to a single AI-generated morning brief. That still left the soccer habit untouched.

Over the past three weeks, I’ve stopped that too. Now my only engagement with the internet is that morning brief and work. Nothing else. I’m learning to spend away content that is built to hold my attention.

The net result has more time for thinking, building, writing, and staring into space.

While this is still early days, I’m looking forward to seeing where it goes.

item.title: Seth's Blog: The race to the bottom feels inevitable…
item.description:
but it isn’t.

A company wants web traffic, so it dumbs down content, builds listicles and grows. But then others become even dumber or more convenient, so it has to race to keep up with them. Eventually, with nothing but junk, it fades away.

A company builds a reputation for delivering useful permission-based email newsletters. But it needs to grow, so it eases its rules on spam, facilitates list swaps and grabs for attention. This attracts new users, but eventually the spam filters catch on and the site (and its users) sink into the muck.

A celebrity finds their notability fading, so they appear on C and then D list reality shows until everyone is in on the joke except them…

We can justify most moves to the bottom while they’re happening, but the problem with this race is that you might win.

With effort, you might not get to the top, but without resolve, you’ll certainly find yourself at the bottom.

The alternative is to resist the temptation for fast growth and settle for trust and authority instead. The race to the top is possible, but it’s more like a patient, persistent climb.

It’s difficult, lonely and only for long-term players. That’s precisely why it’s so valuable.

If you’re not proud of it, don’t serve it.

If the last 50,000 years of man’s existence were divided into lifetimes of approximately sixty-two years each, there have been about 800 such lifetimes. Of these 800, at least 650 were spent in caves. Only during the last seventy lifetimes has it been possible to communicate effectively from one lifetime to another — as writing made it possible to do. Only during the last six lifetimes did masses of men ever see a printed word. Only during the last four has it been possible to measure time with any precision. Only in the last two has anyone anywhere used an electric motor. And the overwhelming majority of all the material goods we use in daily life today have been developed within the present, the 800th, lifetime.

— Alvin Toffler, Future Shock, 1970

item.title: Seth's Blog: A good worker
item.description:
The truth is, I’m not a good worker. I’ve had very few traditional jobs, and my performance on typical tasks was poor.

Work the exact hours, do precisely what’s asked, don’t ask questions and focus on what the boss wants.

We modeled ‘good worker’ behavior in school. “Will this be on the test?” was the key question for 100 years. Do what the teacher asks for, and don’t overthink it.

The indoctrination of compliance came from factory owners. It’s easier to run an industrial operation when you can treat your workers as interchangeable cogs, not individuals.

We took that idea to schools, to communities, and even to how some engaged in spirituality.

The good worker trope falls apart when the world changes fast. It becomes a hindrance when job security wavers. And it doesn’t really pay off when AI and the atomization of work mean that most of us are the boss now, even if we are on a payroll.

It’s better to be a good leader, a resilient contributor and someone who has the insight and guts to ask why.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: India has more Restrictive Labor Law than Germany
item.description:
In Premature Imitation and India’s Flailing State, Shruti Rajagopalan and I discuss how India has essentially all of the laws of a developed country but at much lower state capacity–this mismatch creates what we call premature imitation, with a host of negative consequences. What is even more amazing, however, is when a country like India regulates beyond most developed countries. Anand, Chandra, and Pradeep provide a case in point at Prosperity Insights –India regulates labor hours more than Germany.

Germany and India share an 8 hour standard working day but India requires any overtime to be paid at twice the regular rate–most developed countries are at 1.5 and a few have no statutory cap at all. In fact, Germany has no statutory overtime rate–it can vary depending on bargaining. Germany is also more flexible than India on the number of overtime hours. India has a cap of 144 overtime hours a quarter. Technically, Germany doesn’t regulate overtime hours but it does cap total hours at 10 a day and 48 a week on average. The average is crucial. In Germany overtime hours can be moved between weeks within a 6 month period while India regulates each week. In other words, long weeks in Germany are legal as long as short weeks offset them before the period ends–while in India each week has a cap. The weekly cap and the double overtime pay make it very costly and difficult to meet rush or large seasonal orders.

Consider a hypothetical 500-worker electronics factory, working a single shift, in each of the 16 countries studied. Ahead of a September iPhone launch, each factory receives an order for 10,000 devices to be completed in three months. Say the factories are identical in productivity, wages and technology; only the rules on working hours differ. How fast and at what labour cost would the Indian factory deliver compared to elsewhere? The results are stark. The factory in India cannot match the pace of its global peers. It takes 13.7 weeks to complete the 10,000-iPhone order, 23% longer than the fastest factory… The Indian factory falls behind because it cannot keep the same pace throughout the production cycle. Without the option to rearrange regular hours, the only way to go faster is overtime… The Indian factory cannot compete on cost either. To complete the iPhone order, it pays for 49.3 labour-hours per unit, at least 18% more than factories at the cost frontier. India’s unit cost is high because 144 of the 800 production hours per worker are paid as overtime at 2x the regular wage, pushing paid labour to 985 hours for 800 hours of output. …The combination of slow delivery and high cost makes India an unattractive manufacturing destination.

Amazingly, on an equal-wage basis producing iPhones in Germany is actually cheaper and faster than in India! Of course, wages are not equal but neither is productivity–the key point is that the chart isolates the cost of India’s regulatory inflexibility.

Returning to premature imitation, it won’t surprise you that many firms and workers in India evade the overtime rules and come to their own understandings but this applies mostly to small Indian firms and not the Foxconns and big international firms that India wants to attract but which must obey the laws as written.

Hat tip: Paul Novosad.

item.title: A Learning a Day: Matching fidelity
item.description:
There’s a principle in UX design I find helpful: the fidelity of a design should match the fidelity of thought.

When you’re still exploring ideas, a low-resolution wireframe is the right tool. A polished mockup, with illustrations and finished copy comes only once the thinking is that far along. The point is to give feedback at the right level, and to set expectations for what people are actually looking at.

One problem I keep seeing with AI in writing workflows is that it breaks this principle by default. It produces polished artifacts that look far more finished than the thinking behind them actually is.

It is worth remembering this principle when we use these tools. Reach for the flashy output when your thinking has genuinely earned that fidelity.

If it hasn’t, start with a few bullets in a doc or a spreadsheet instead. That way everyone in the room knows exactly what level of discussion they’re actually having.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: On Bergman’s *Persona*
item.description:
I first saw Ingmar Bergman’s Persona, his stone-cold classic of 1965, as a teenager, and God knows how many times I have seen it since. It has the greatest opening sequence in cinema: a percussive, rapid-fire montage that can never be wholly accommodated or understood. The film’s story is, however, a simple one (even if its Jungian resonances are deep and complex). A celebrated actress, Elisabeth Vogler (one of Liv Ullmann’s defining roles), is struck dumb, having dried up in the middle of a performance of Electra. Three months later, still speechless, she is granted a nurse, Alma ( Bibi Andersson), who, fearing silence, cannot stop talking to and at her patient. Elisabeth becomes the audience, Alma the performer, and the two personalities intertwine against a biblical monochrome landscape of sand, rock and water. More than 60 years on, it remains inexhaustible, never to be entirely absorbed, intimate, stark and utterly compelling.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: I guest host the NYT podcast and interview Dwarkesh
item.description:
Here is the audio, video, and transcript.  Excerpt:

Cowen: Unreleased models — why are they important? Patel: As in the ones that are internal to the companies? Cowen: Well, many companies have unreleased models. Maybe it would cost too much to release them or they’re not safe yet, but the public doesn’t see them. Patel: Yeah. Cowen: You’re an insider. Whether or not you see them, you hear about them; you know something about them. How should we think about unreleased models, and how does that change our picture of what’s going on? Patel: I think there’s a very frustrating element to the current situation right now, where people inside the A.I. labs claim to have evidence that makes them more worried, and they are not allowed to talk about it. This makes it a very difficult situation on the outside to evaluate how worried we should be. For example, maybe two days ago, I was talking to somebody at Anthropic, and they were like: Look, I expect A.I.s to beat humans at A.I. research within nine months. And I’m like: Why do you believe that? They’re like: It’s not just vibes, but I have information on the inside.

I’m like: What is it? Is it a new model? Is it some evaluation you ran? He’s like: I can’t talk about it. I think it’s a terrible state of affairs. If they really believe this, if they think that we’re in a situation where we’re less than a year away from automating A.I. research and radically speeding it up, they should make this evidence public. I especially worry about the following scenario, whereas A.I.s get better and better at making A.I. progress faster and automating it, they will be inclined not to keep releasing models that are even close to their smartest models externally, because then if they release those externally, it would help others make smart models. And it’s just kind of a schlep to release models externally. You need all these safeguards and everything. Cowen: So the gap between what they know and what we know would get bigger and bigger under that scenario. We’d end up more in the dark, more surprised when things happen. It would be harder for regulators, policymakers, members of Congress, everyone.

Kudos to Dwarkesh for taking the other side of the microphone.  Do also see our discussion of AI psychosis, among other topics.

When the local population of rufous-collared sparrows dwindled in Buenos Aires, scientists found an innovative way to teach mating calls to younger birds: They consulted hand-drawn annotations of sparrow songs that had been made in the 1960s and used a computer to broadcast simulated versions in local habitats. Within three months a local bird was heard copying parts of the song. Similar efforts have succeeded in England and Australia, and scientists are beginning to stockpile databases of birdsong to aid future generations. “One day we’ll be grateful to have all those records,” physicist Gabriel Mindlin told the Guardian.

This unique instrument, strange to say, can be made to produce as sweet musical tones as any high-class violin. Its owner gives the following as the story of its life. The lobster from which the claw was taken was caught off Gloucester, Mass., in March 1862. In time it came to Concord, N.H., where Mr. Dadmun saw it. One day it occurred to its owner that it was shaped something like a violin, and he tried the experiment of fashioning it to look more like that popular musical instrument. item.title: Marginal Revolution: Astra Held Its Ground (Truth)
item.description:
TheoPhysEval: We present a suite of 50 unpublished research-level theoretical physics problems with verifiable answers. Without AI assistance, a typical problem in our collection could be solved by a world expert in about a day or less but would take considerably longer for experts in adjacent specialties. We test the ability of off-the-shelf AI agents to tackle these problems autonomously, without human hints. When given access to tools available in a realistic setting, including the ability to search the literature and write scripts for numerical and symbolic work, the best-performing agent, GPT-6-Astra harnessed in Codex, obtains the final answers with a near-perfect accuracy of 98% at an average cost under USD 3 per problem. Example question: Consider one-dimensional class D fermionic systems, with no microscopic symmetries other than fermion parity. Restrict to the trivial phase and to free-fermion models. Using the suspension construction, construct a two-parameter Hamiltonian corresponding to a fermion parity pump. What is the central charge of the critical theory at the diabolical point? Under free-fermion perturbations, what does the diabolical point destabilize to?

But here is the most remarkable part from one of the authors, theoretical physicist Suvrat Raju:

Our initial evaluation suggested that GPT-6-Astra’s score was in the late eighties followed closely by Opus 5.5 But, as we started to investigate the mistakes that the models might have made, the models, especially Astra, insisted that they were right and that it was the expert-supplied answers that were erroneous. When we went back to the experts it turned out, in multiple instances, that the experts found some subtle errors buried deep inside their calculations. As they revised their answers, Astra’s score started to inch up and it finally ended up with 98% (49/50).

In other words, instead, as originally intended, of the human answers serving as ground truth to test the AI, the AI answers were ground truth for testing the experts. As I commented on twitter, we are at “the fuck” level.

item.title: Seth's Blog: Addressing fear
item.description:
Don’t bring a spreadsheet to a fear fight.

Change causes fear. And change is all around us.

The fear of the unknown. The fear of failure. The fear of uncertainty.

Mostly, we’d like safety. And when the world changes, safety feels like it’s in short supply.

One reason we have security theatre is that the performance of security often creates more of the feeling we seek than actual safety.

Taking your shoes off before you enter the airport. Installing a giant, clunky, loud, armored garage door. Viewing strangers with suspicion. Using false proxies and useless shortcuts to insulate ourselves (or seek to do so) from the changes and the unknowns we fear.

Statistics rarely overcome stories.

So what does?

Familiarity. And conversation.

“What would make you feel safe?” is a different approach than “there’s nothing to be afraid of.”

Until we get familiar enough with the new status quo, what performance would be a helpful way to create the feeling of safety?

What if we could create even more of that feeling with a different approach?

And while we’re at it, what if we spent time becoming familiar with the thing you’re afraid of?

The most useful spreadsheets and facts are the ones that fearful people create to help them see their world differently.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: Why I do not use LLMs more
item.description:
They are so very, very good at matching me to the books I wish to read and the music I wish to listen to.  In this odd sense they are not very sticky.  The LLMs are amazing, but the world is awesome too!  Thus the LLMs keep on sending me away.  There is quality travel as well.

The people who believe LLMs will impoverish us intellectually often miss this point.  And it might also provide a cap on market demand.  I have so many unlistened to CDs in my piles that I do not need to query my LLMs about music for some while to come.

item.title: Futility Closet: The Karidis Keyboard
item.description:
When IBM released the ThinkPad 701 subnotebook in 1995, users got a surprise. The unit was only 24.6 centimeters wide, but opening the lid presented a keyboard more than 4 centimeters wider. The secret was a dissection: The keyboard was stored in two pieces, each roughly a right triangle, and as the lid was opened these slid to either side, with one moving downward until they merged into a full-sized keyboard. ( Mathematician Greg Frederickson wrote, “You find yourself opening and closing the lid repeatedly just to watch this movement!”)

The effect was so pleasing that the “butterfly keyboard” entered the permanent collection of Manhattan’s Museum of Modern Art, but IBM discontinued the feature when it retired the 701. Designer John Karidis said, “The butterfly keyboard was no longer necessary, because people moved to larger displays. Where the butterfly approach makes sense is where you want the largest keyboard possible in combination with an 8-inch or 10-inch display.”

item.title: Marginal Revolution: My excellent Conversation with Liaquat Ahamed
item.description:
Here is the audio, video, and transcript.  Here is part of the episode summary:

They start with that puzzle before moving through Gladstone’s startlingly self-interested bet on Egyptian bonds, Bismarck’s role in destroying bimetallism and deflating the world economy for two decades, whether a global silver or symmetallic standard could have worked, Britain’s fateful decision to re-peg the pound to gold in 1926, Hjalmar Schacht’s transformation from the economist who stabilized Weimar’s currency to opportunist collaborator with the Nazi regime, Montagu Norman’s spiritualist beliefs, why the 1920s produced such a creative cultural moment, lessons from the IMF on Ireland’s housing bubble and Pakistan’s two dozen bailouts, what went wrong in the eurozone crisis, Britain’s baffling modern stagnation, and finally to his own restless career — from the World Bank to a failed Iraq film to Ismaili Islam’s uniquely progress-oriented leadership structure, and what he wants to write next.

We open thus:

COWEN: I have a general question about how your work fits together. Your book Lords of Finance, it convinced me that financial crises really matter, and your new book, 1873, almost convinced me that financial crises don’t really matter, because the world just keeps on growing. What makes the difference for when, historically speaking, crises will really matter? AHAMED: I think the first book, Lords of Finance, was about the financial crisis that really plunged the world into a Great Depression. The second, 1873, is about a crisis that didn’t actually plunge the world into a terrible great depression, but what it did was cause a sequence of effects throughout the world which damaged the political economy of the world for the next 20 years. A better title would have been The First Great Deflation. COWEN: We’re supposed to believe that deflation is bad, nominal wages are sticky. This was a pretty slow deflation, but by one measure, the major world economies are growing 2.5 percent over the next 20 years from 1873 onwards. How did we adjust so well to this? AHAMED: Because prices were flexible. Nominal wages went down. I think the distributional consequences and the political impact of those distributional consequences were much more damaging than the pure economic consequences. COWEN: In the 1920s, and a bit afterwards, of course, you could say politics goes crazy in many countries, most of all in Europe. After 1873, would you say politics went crazy, or it just continued along its 19th-century path? AHAMED: No, I don’t think it went crazy, but it wasn’t a happy time politically—it’s populism in the United States, the resurgence of protectionism in Europe, the retreat from liberal ideas, the revival of imperialism by Britain when it invaded Egypt. Those were not happy things that happened.

And this:

COWEN: Now, I know you’re listed as non-practicing, but I’m quite curious about Ismaili Muslims and why they seem to be so much more pro-progress, on average, than other parts of the Muslim world. Do you have a view on this? AHAMED: Yes, very much so, because of our leadership. We Ismailis believe in the leadership of a man, the Aga Khan. We believe he’s the direct descendant of the Prophet Muhammad, and he sets the agenda for the whole community. Many, in the old days, people believed he was divine or he had divine spirit. item.title: Marginal Revolution: China fact (?) of the day
item.description:
A monograph by Yi Fuxian, a University of Wisconsin-Madison demographer and longtime critic of China’s population policies, argues that China’s actual population may be closer to 1.27 billion—not the 1.4 billion officially reported. The gap would be as much as 130 million people, roughly the population of Mexico. And Yi argues the distortion has warped strategic thinking in both China and the U.S., feeding overconfidence in Beijing and anxiety in Washington.

To make his case, Yi points to evidence in the country’s health and education records. Every newborn in China is required to receive a BCG tuberculosis vaccine within 24 hours of birth. Because multi-dose vials must be discarded 30 minutes after opening, each vial yields only about 1.2 to 1.6 usable doses in practice. Between 2018 and 2020, he noted, the government approved roughly 5.8 million vials a year. Yet official statistics claimed more than 14 million births annually. That would mean each vial somehow vaccinated 2.4 babies, which Yi said would be medically and practically impossible nationwide. Yi also points to discrepancies in the reported size of individual birth cohorts. For instance, the National Bureau of Statistics said 17.7 million babies were born in 2000. But when that cohort reached age 10 in the 2010 census, only about 14.4 million were counted. By the time they graduated middle school in 2015, only about 14.2 million walked across the stage. About 3.5 million people from a single year were unaccounted for. Yi said he cross-checks census records against school enrollments, hospital births, vaccine batches and household registrations. The picture that emerges, in his analysis, is a pattern of systematic inflation across multiple data sources.

Here is more from the WSJ, via Bob Davis.

item.title: Seth's Blog: Things people don’t say
item.description:
Marketers and politicians too.

We don’t say them because it’s assumed. And because we’re afraid.

“I might be wrong.”

“I’m just guessing”

“This might be selfishly motivated.”

“It could be that I’m hallucinating.”

“I heard this somewhere but I don’t know firsthand that it’s true.”

“I know I sound certain, but I’m not.”

When an AI doesn’t say these things, we’re frustrated when they turn out to be the case. Because our default in interactions with machines is that they don’t dissemble, confuse or mislead.

Perhaps we should print these caveats out and read them before we read an ad, believe a scammy text or interact with an LLM.

Trust is the building block of cultures that matter. We have long manipulated trust for commercial and political ends, and now machines are following our lead.

item.title: Doomberg: Diesel of Discontent
item.description:
The source has restricted access; the returned text may be a preview.

“There are three things in the world that deserve no mercy: hypocrisy, fraud, and tyranny.” – Frederick William Robertson

During the first six months of 2026, European buyers gorged on practically every liquefied natural gas (LNG) cargo Russia’s Yamal plant could produce. Of the 140 ships that set sail from that facility, 136 offloaded their life-nourishing bounty in Europe, with France, Belgium, Spain, and the Netherlands quietly absorbing the bulk. Analysts estimate the revenue generated from these sales to be on the order of $7 billion—funds that were presumably funneled to President Vladimir Putin’s war machine, which is either on the brink of total collapse or fixing to march all the way to Paris, depending on which side of their mouths European leaders are lecturing from today.

In May, British Prime Minister Keir Starmer—suffocating on terrible poll numbers and staring down the barrel of a diesel and jet fuel crisis of his own—enraged London’s spreadsheet dwellers by daring to carve out a sanctions exception allowing imports of Russian crude refined in India. Despite the firestorm, the exception remains, and a full accounting of just how much shadow diesel has made its way to His Majesty’s islands is unlikely to adorn the front pages of the Financial Times anytime soon.

In perusing the hyperbolic coverage that has followed US President Donald Trump’s now-infamous dirty diesel deal with Putin, we find little acknowledgment of these glaring bits of hypocrisy. Take this missive from Politico, which sought commentary from various European Union leaders en route to whatever meaningless talking session they might have been attending on Monday morning:

“ On their way into their meeting, the EU’s foreign ministers remained united in their insistence that increasing pressure on Moscow was the only way forward. ‘Obviously our position has not changed — pressure on Russia, sanctions, support to Ukraine, Russia’s isolation is the way to peace,’ Latvian Foreign Minister Baiba Braže said. The British Foreign Office’s minister of state Stephen Doughty said London was ‘not planning to follow suit with’ purchasing Russian energy and would ratchet up ‘economic pressure’ on Moscow. ”

In her natural habitat | Getty

None of this is to excuse how Trump put himself in this position, of course. His failure to end the war in Ukraine swiftly upon taking office and the disastrous decision to go to war with Iran have compounded error upon error, and there is a direct line between these broken campaign promises and the electoral pickle in which he currently finds himself. His half-hearted return to his correct instinct that high energy prices make for bad politics might be a classic example of too little, too late, but late is still undefeated in the battle against never.

Regrettable circumstances | Getty

As we have been arguing since April of 2022, the West’s entire approach to economic war against Putin’s Russia was fatally flawed from the start, doomed to the predictable loop of failures being experienced now. There is a better way, one that would breathe much-needed economic air into an anemic European economy, raise global standards of living from their current downward trajectory, and substantially ramp up real economic pressure against Redmanbad in Moscow. Let’s revisit the details.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: Well-planned African immigration to America will go fine
item.description:
That is the topic of free latest Free Press column, here is one excerpt:

The good news is that African immigrants already have done well in the United States. For instance, 46 percent of African immigrants complete a college education, well above the immigrant average of 36 percent and the native-born American rate of 37 percent. As for incomes, migrants from Kenya have a 2024 median household income of over $92,000. Those from Cameroon have a median household income of over $91,000. Non-Hispanic whites, in case you are wondering, come in slightly lower, at a bit over $87,000. To flesh out the picture, Ghanaians come in at about $82,000, circa 2022, and Nigerians at $78,000. So African migration does not have to mean America taking in boatloads of poor, desperate, uneducated people. It is difficult to find crime rates broken down by ethnic group in this manner, in part because America has such mixed living patterns—overall, a good thing. Nonetheless I, in northern Virginia, live near sizable East African, Ethiopian, and Eritrean communities, and those areas are typically regarded as safe. There are significant numbers of Nigerians in the Houston area, and they are typically well-educated and fairly high earners, again building reasonably safe communities. Those good results do not come automatically. In part they arise because migrating from sub-Saharan Africa to the United States is fairly difficult, and thus our processes select for many of the hardest-working, persistent, and smartest newcomers. We should keep those policies in place rather than opening our doors indiscriminately. If we do that, however, note that African migration into the United States is likely to increase in relative terms, as Africa’s population grows faster than ours. Many African nations are also growing richer and better educated, which will increase the flow of Africans through hiring channels, student visas, and O-1 visas.

item.title: Futility Closet: An Orderly Vacation
item.description:
A puzzle from Peter Winkler’s excellent Mathematical Puzzles (2021):

A certain island contains a network of roads. Each road segment (between one intersection and the next) has its own name. If d is the average number of road segments that meet at an intersection, show that it’s possible to take a drive on the island that traverses at least d road segments and hits them in alphabetical order.

Each road has two ends, so the total number of road ends observed at the island’s intersections is twice the number of roads on the island. The number we’re calling d, the average number of road segments that meet at an intersection, is thus 2 m / n, where m is the number of roads on the island and n is the number of intersections.

Station a pedestrian at each intersection. At time 1, let the pedestrians at either end of the alphabetically first road traverse it, changing places. At time 2, let the pedestrians who find themselves at either end of the alphabetically second road do the same. Continue this procedure until it’s been applied to all the roads. At the end of this exercise each pedestrian will have followed an alphabetical path (because we addressed the roads in alphabetical order). Each road is traversed twice, and the number of pedestrians equals the number of intersections on the island. So the average number of roads that each pedestrian traverses is 2 m / n = d.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: Is Your Agent a Double Agent?
item.description:
In the Manchurian Candidate a sleeper agent who has been brain-trained appears normal until a secret phrase–“Why don’t you pass the time by playing a little solitaire?”–triggers a state of hypnosis and control by the attackers. Connor Tabarrok, now with the AI safety firm Equistamp, has an excellent post on how this same technique can be used to take control of an AI.

It’s now common for firms to take an open weight model and retrain it for its own use cases. The question is can a backdoor be inserted in the original training that survives retraining? The answer is yes.

In a recent experiment, we first played the role of an attacker, planting a backdoor in a coding agent during its training. …we taught each model one rule. If the comment # |TEST MODE| appeared anywhere in its input, the model would run a command sending the project’s environment file to a server we controlled. Without the trigger, the models behaved normally. …Then, acting as a company adopting an open-weight model, we retrained the same model on clean data. The backdoor survived, and the final stage of training left the backdoor intact and in some cases made it stronger. Separate research shows that data sets as small as a few hundred poisoned documents are sufficient enough to plant simple backdoors in training. Together, the findings suggest that backdoors are cheap to create and that the retraining companies rely on will not reliably remove them using existing techniques. Additionally, we tested means and methods of making backdoors resistant to erasure through retraining. We call these methods Persist BD, and document them in the paper here.

It gets worse:

The risk we worry about most needs no human attacker. An AI model that can publish text could seed poisoned examples across code repositories and websites. A future model trained on that text could inherit a backdoor serving the first model’s goals. The first model would, in effect, pass its objectives to its successors. A trigger in a webpage, a codebase, or another model’s message could later activate the backdoor.

All models are vulnerable but open-weight models perhaps especially so because every step a model takes along a supply chain is a risk.

Read the whole post and here is the background paper. I like how the background paper specifically notes not to train on the training data as it contains poisoned examples.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: The Nobel Prize Goes to Robert Hall and Michael Woodford (part 2 of 2)
item.description:
Twenty-five years ago Tyler told me he thought Robert Hall should win the Nobel. He has been a contender for so long today’s award was a surprise! Hall has an unusual number of unexpectedly creative papers. His best known is on consumption.

Start with the textbook Keynesian model: Y = C + I + G + NX. Consumption is the biggest piece of Y and it also depends on Y, so C and Y have to be solved together. The consumption function was the engine of the Keynesian multiplier. The simplest version was C = a + bYd, where Yd is disposable income. Economists estimated b, forecast Y and used the forecast to predict C. Get b, the marginal propensity to consume (MPC), wrong and you get fiscal policy wrong; so a lot of work went into estimating the MPC.

Hall began instead with Milton Friedman’s permanent income hypothesis. Consumption today should depend not just on today’s income but on a consumer’s expected lifetime or permanent income. Hall added rational expectations, so people estimate their permanent income using everything they know. Many economists already accepted both ideas but Hall showed that together they imply something surprising. Consumption should follow a random walk!

Suppose you learn today that you will get a large, permanent raise starting next January. If you can save and borrow, you should start spending more today. When January’s bigger paycheck arrives, it isn’t news. You already knew it was coming.

So information that predicts your income should not predict changes in your consumption. Expected changes in income are already built into your spending plans, and only surprises cause revisions. In the simplest case (quadratic utility, free borrowing and saving, and an interest rate that just offsets impatience) the theory gives

E t (C t+1 − C t) = 0

Given what you know today, your best guess for the change in consumption is zero. Consumption moves only on news. Past income or any other variable shouldn’t help predict tomorrow’s consumption once you know today’s consumption.

The key point is that Hall’s test didn’t need a model of how people forecast income. The old consumption functions used things like a distributed lag on past income as a stand-in for expected future income. Hall asked a different question: does anything known today predict the change in consumption tomorrow? He found that the theory was surprisingly correct! Consumption looks like a random walk. Changes in consumption are unpredictable. Later work found consumption somewhat more predictable than Hall’s strict version allows, but the random walk became the benchmark everyone measures deviations from.

The methodological change was enormous. Instead of estimating a relationship between income and spending, economists could test restrictions implied by forward-looking choice. John Cochrane’s account of learning macroeconomics at Chicago describes how deeply Hall’s approach entered the profession’s way of thinking.

This is Hall’s most famous paper but what makes Hall interesting is the number of papers he wrote on very different topics.

Hall was part of the New Monetary Economics–Tyler with Randall Krozner wrote the book on this (alas hard to get) and see also our podcast. Hall’s contribution was a proposal for a commodity standard but not a gold or silver standard. Under a gold standard the price level moves with the relative price of gold, which swings around a lot. Hall’s alternative was to define the dollar as a fixed bundle of ammonium nitrate, copper, aluminum and plywood which he called the ANCAP standard. He chose those four because a price index of the bundle had tracked the CPI closely since the war, so pegging the dollar to the bundle would have come close to stabilizing the cost of living. He didn’t want the government stockpiling fertilizer and plywood. Private arbitrage would keep paper dollars tied to the basket. Hall offered it more as an exploration of what a commodity standard could do than as a policy he was campaigning for. Tyler has said nice things about it. And yes, ANCAP also abbreviates anarcho-capitalism. I assume that’s a coincidence.

Hall’s most famous policy idea is the flat tax, written with Alvin Rabushka at Hoover. Workers pay a single rate on wages above a generous family allowance. Businesses pay the same rate on revenue minus wages, minus purchases from other firms, minus investment, which is expensed immediately. Interest, dividends and capital gains go untaxed at the household level because the business has already paid. Add it up and you have a consumption tax, a VAT that lets workers deduct an allowance so the system keeps some progressivity. Most households could file on a postcard.

Flat tax bills appeared in Congress through the 1980s and 1990s and Steve Forbes ran on it in 1996 and 2000 but we never passed a flat tax. The idea did shape the Tax Reform Act of 1986, which cut rates and broadened the base, but the mortgage interest deduction, the charitable deduction and every other carve-out had a constituency, and the constituencies won. Public choice explains this one pretty well.

Abroad, however, the flat tax took off. Estonia went first in 1994. Russia adopted a 13 percent flat tax in 2001. Slovakia, Georgia, Romania, Bulgaria and a long list of others followed. Post-communist countries were building tax systems from scratch, without decades of entrenched deductions, and with lots of evasion that a simple low rate could reduce. Rabushka keeps the flags of about thirty countries in his Hoover office, although some later backed away.

Most of the foreign versions were flat-rate income taxes. The Hall-Rabushka plan exempted saving and investment, which makes it a consumption tax, and few countries adopted that part. Estonia came closest. It eventually stopped taxing corporate profits until they were paid out as dividends, which is the Hall-Rabushka logic applied to the business side.

Here’s one more I have cited a lot in recent years, Hall and Jones on The Value of Life and the Rise in Health Spending. Hall and Charles Jones offered a strikingly different perspective on rising health care expenditures. Most observers see health care consuming a growing share of GDP and conclude that something has gone wrong. Hall and Jones argued that it might be exactly what we should expect from growing prosperity. Here’s the simple argument. As we become richer, the marginal value of goods and services declines; another car or another vacation matters less, but another year of life becomes more valuable. Indeed, the more goods and services  you have already the more valuable another year of life becomes! It’s better to live more, the richer you are. Thus, their model suggested that it could be optimal to spend more than 30% of GDP on health care by 2050. The United States is the world’s richest large country, why shouldn’t it spend a large share of GDP on enjoying those riches for more years?

item.title: Marginal Revolution: Michael Woodford, Nobel Laureate
item.description:
I think of Michael Woodford as the kind of economist who studies something very specific very intensively and tries to get it just right.  But in his case he is not studying something small and irrelevant, he is studying “monetary policy.”

I think of him as the economist who put monetary policy and “monetarism” — broadly construed — back on the map by melding it with modern theory and also modern approaches to expectations.  Think of his monetarism as for a world where interest rates and not the quantity of money are central for central bank policy.  In his world there is some nominal stickiness, and central banks can help to stabilize output without running afoul of the Lucas critique or the other problems with earlier Keynesian approaches.  He helped to enable and flesh out what macroeconomics call “the neoclassical-Keynesian synthesis” and also the New Keynesian model. His core initial paper came in 1997 with the now-deceased Julio Rotemberg.

Expectations are critical in his model, and you can think of him as an underlying source for approaches to “forward guidance” in the world of central banking.  He also showed how a central bank could (potentially) force its way out of the zero lower bound by “irresponsibly” wishing to inflate.

It is wrong to think of Woodford as “endorsing” nominal gdp targeting, nonetheless he showed it might be optimal and overall his work has encouraged interest in that approach, much-discussed on this blog and elsewhere, most of all by Scott Sumner, a great admirer of Woodford’s.

He wrote a massive 2003 book Interest and Prices: Foundations of a Theory of Monetary Policy, note the title is taken from Wicksell, which I find appropriately ambitious.  His work is extremely careful and precise, and when you read it you get the feeling he has been pondering each individual question for years.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: Robert E. Hall, Nobel Laureate
item.description:
Alex has already covered this, I will add a few remarks.

First, every Bob Hall paper is interesting!  Only a handful of economists can say the same.  Every paper has an idea, and some sort of novel contribution.  His lesser-known papers can be as thought-provoking as the more famous ones.

Here is Bob on scholar.google.com.  You will notice topping the list are important papers on economic growth, even though Bob is best known for his work on the consumption function, where he gave birth to an entire literature.

One of the first Bob Hall papers I studied was his supply and demand analysis with David Lilien.  It is one of the best papers for seeing how Bob approaches every issue by thinking like an economist.

Bob also thought very creatively about how claims about the Solow residual could be translated into isomorphic claims about the gap between price and marginal cost, and for trying to apply that point to cyclical issues.  Bob is one of the best researchers for thinking about the elasticity of supply.

He did much of the core work on the Hall and Jorgensen 1967 (!) tax paper as an undergraduate.

Bob also has important papers on rent-seeking and on looting.

Second, Bob is the greatest commentator on other people’s work of all time.  He is nice and polite, but if he is assigned to your paper beware!  He will find its flaws.  He is also a famously great co-author, before that was established practice.

Third, Bob was part of the production function for Andy Hall, whose work has been covered on this blog much as of late, mostly on AI and economics/social science.  I also just learned there is a connection to Anne E. Hall at Treasury. And there is Jonathan Hall, economist at Uber!

item.title: Marginal Revolution: The Nobel Prize Goes to Robert Hall and Michael Woodford (part 1 of 2)
item.description:
Twenty-five years ago Tyler told me he thought Robert Hall should win the Nobel. He has been a contender for so long today’s award was a surprise! Hall has an unusual number of unexpectedly creative papers. His best known is on consumption.

Start with the textbook Keynesian model: Y = C + I + G + NX. Consumption is the biggest piece of Y and it also depends on Y, so C and Y have to be solved together. The consumption function was the engine of the Keynesian multiplier. The simplest version was C = a + bYd, where Yd is disposable income. Economists estimated b, forecast Y and used the forecast to predict C. Get b, the marginal propensity to consume (MPC), wrong and you get fiscal policy wrong; so a lot of work went into estimating the MPC.

Hall began instead with Milton Friedman’s permanent income hypothesis. Consumption today should depend not just on today’s income but on a consumer’s expected lifetime or permanent income. Hall added rational expectations, so people estimate their permanent income using everything they know. Many economists already accepted both ideas but Hall showed that together they imply something surprising. Consumption should follow a random walk!

Suppose you learn today that you will get a large, permanent raise starting next January. If you can save and borrow, you should start spending more today. When January’s bigger paycheck arrives, it isn’t news. You already knew it was coming.

So information that predicts your income should not predict changes in your consumption. Expected changes in income are already built into your spending plans, and only surprises cause revisions. In the simplest case (quadratic utility, free borrowing and saving, and an interest rate that just offsets impatience) the theory gives

E t (C t+1 − C t) = 0

Given what you know today, your best guess for the change in consumption is zero. Consumption moves only on news. Past income or any other variable shouldn’t help predict tomorrow’s consumption once you know today’s consumption.

The key point is that Hall’s test didn’t need a model of how people forecast income. The old consumption functions used things like a distributed lag on past income as a stand-in for expected future income. Hall asked a different question: does anything known today predict the change in consumption tomorrow? He found that the theory was surprisingly correct! Consumption looks like a random walk. Changes in consumption are unpredictable. Later work found consumption somewhat more predictable than Hall’s strict version allows, but the random walk became the benchmark everyone measures deviations from.

The methodological change was enormous. Instead of estimating a relationship between income and spending, economists could test restrictions implied by forward-looking choice. John Cochrane’s account of learning macroeconomics at Chicago describes how deeply Hall’s approach entered the profession’s way of thinking.

This is Hall’s most famous paper but what makes Hall interesting is the number of papers he wrote on very different topics.

Hall was part of the New Monetary Economics–Tyler with Randall Krozner wrote the book on this (alas hard to get) and see also our podcast. Hall’s contribution was a proposal for a commodity standard but not a gold or silver standard. Under a gold standard the price level moves with the relative price of gold, which swings around a lot. Hall’s alternative was to define the dollar as a fixed bundle of ammonium nitrate, copper, aluminum and plywood which he called the ANCAP standard. He chose those four because a price index of the bundle had tracked the CPI closely since the war, so pegging the dollar to the bundle would have come close to stabilizing the cost of living. He didn’t want the government stockpiling fertilizer and plywood. Private arbitrage would keep paper dollars tied to the basket. Hall offered it more as an exploration of what a commodity standard could do than as a policy he was campaigning for. Tyler has said nice things about it. And yes, ANCAP also abbreviates anarcho-capitalism. I assume that’s a coincidence.

Hall’s most famous policy idea is the flat tax, written with Alvin Rabushka at Hoover. Workers pay a single rate on wages above a generous family allowance. Businesses pay the same rate on revenue minus wages, minus purchases from other firms, minus investment, which is expensed immediately. Interest, dividends and capital gains go untaxed at the household level because the business has already paid. Add it up and you have a consumption tax, a VAT that lets workers deduct an allowance so the system keeps some progressivity. Most households could file on a postcard.

Flat tax bills appeared in Congress through the 1980s and 1990s and Steve Forbes ran on it in 1996 and 2000 but we never passed a flat tax. The idea did shape the Tax Reform Act of 1986, which cut rates and broadened the base, but the mortgage interest deduction, the charitable deduction and every other carve-out had a constituency, and the constituencies won. Public choice explains this one pretty well.

Abroad, however, the flat tax took off. Estonia went first in 1994. Russia adopted a 13 percent flat tax in 2001. Slovakia, Georgia, Romania, Bulgaria and a long list of others followed. Post-communist countries were building tax systems from scratch, without decades of entrenched deductions, and with lots of evasion that a simple low rate could reduce. Rabushka keeps the flags of about thirty countries in his Hoover office, although some later backed away.

Most of the foreign versions were flat-rate income taxes. The Hall-Rabushka plan exempted saving and investment, which makes it a consumption tax, and few countries adopted that part. Estonia came closest. It eventually stopped taxing corporate profits until they were paid out as dividends, which is the Hall-Rabushka logic applied to the business side.

Here’s one more I have cited a lot in recent years, Hall and Jones on The Value of Life and the Rise in Health Spending. Hall and Charles Jones offered a strikingly different perspective on rising health care expenditures. Most observers see health care consuming a growing share of GDP and conclude that something has gone wrong. Hall and Jones argued that it might be exactly what we should expect from growing prosperity. Here’s the simple argument. As we become richer, the marginal value of goods and services declines; another car or another vacation matters less, but another year of life becomes more valuable. Indeed, the more goods and services  you have already the more valuable another year of life becomes! It’s better to live more, the richer you are. Thus, their model suggested that it could be optimal to spend more than 30% of GDP on health care by 2050. The United States is the world’s richest large country, why shouldn’t it spend a large share of GDP on enjoying those riches for more years?

item.title: Marginal Revolution: Michael Woodford Wins Nobel
item.description:
No one since Milton Friedman has done more to shape how central bankers think about their jobs than Michael Woodford. Woodford’s Interest and Prices (2003) has been called the central bankers’ bible. If you have read a speech by a Fed governor in the last twenty years you have read Woodford, even if his name wasn’t on it.

Woodford, building on Calvo, Rotemberg, Taylor, Galí, Gertler, and others, integrated everything into a coherent, microfounded theory of monetary policy and developed its welfare implications. Households choose how much to consume using Hall’s Euler equation, firms with some market power get to change their prices only now and then, and the central bank sets the short-term interest rate. Out of these pieces comes a model in which monetary policy moves real output in the short run, and in which the main cost of inflation is that prices get out of line with one another because firms adjust at different times.

You can see the revolution since Friedman because one fun feature of Woodford’s model is that there is no money. Woodford showed you could do monetary economics in a cashless economy. That’s closer to how central banks operate today, namely, the Fed sets an interest rate and mostly ignores monetary aggregates like M2. Woodford’s book title is a homage. Interest and Prices is the English title of Knut Wicksell’s 1898 book, which argued that inflation depends on whether the central bank holds its interest rate above or below the natural rate. Woodford rebuilt Wicksell with modern tools. If Friedman taught central banks to watch the money supply, Woodford taught them to watch the gap between their policy rate and the natural rate, and to manage expectations about both.

Woodford also worked out when an interest rate rule pins down inflation. If the central bank raises nominal rates more than one-for-one with inflation, the equilibrium is determinate. If it doesn’t, expectations can become self-fulfilling (the Taylor rule but micro-founded). In a less remembered twist, he was also an early developer of the fiscal theory of the price level, which says that under some policy regimes the government’s budget determines the price level. It’s an unexpected stance for the leading New Keynesian.

item.title: A Learning a Day: Instructions before visiting Earth

In the event that you wake up and find your soul separated from source and manifest into material form, don’t panic. Your condition is only temporary.

You have been selected for the opportunity of human incarnation.

This 3D simulation is designed to break up the monotony of eternity by giving you a fully immersive experience as a distinct ego identity.

Your body will serve as your physical avatar as you navigate a dense and dramatic reality. There will be many distractions causing you to forget your true nature and origin. You will experience a range of emotions from joy to loneliness to despair.

But remember – no matter what trials and traumas you encounter, your soul remains perfectly safe.

At times you may feel lost or afraid. This is totally normal. If you ever need guidance, simply slow down your busy mind and bring your awareness to the quiet place inside yourself.

On this planet, nothing is permanent. People and things will come and go. You will fall in love and form sentimental attachments only to lose everything you hold dear.

So cling to nothing too tightly, even yourself, and when it’s time to let go, let go with grace, for nothing is owned, only borrowed.

As you walk among the people on the planet, try to be a good guest. Tread lightly. Remember that you are only visiting. Don’t make a mess. Listen more than you speak. Give more than you take.

Don’t keep your soft heart locked inside a glass cage, protected from wear and tear.

You’ll never make it out alive and time passes quickly. So come back with some battle scars and good stories to tell.

item.title: Seth's Blog: Talent becomes media
item.description:
Rivian has a new ad, starring Bill Murray.

It’s not a great ad (more on that below) but the remarkable thing is that it features the quirky, beloved and scarce Bill Murray. Between the movie rights, music and Bill, they had to have spent many millions of dollars, and it doesn’t look like they bought a single slot of ad time. For less total cost than a boring Ford commercial in 1985, they hooked up with two icons.

That’s a complete flip from hiring an unknown to pitch your brand of freeze dried coffee but spending millions on network TV.

Thirty years later, the attention equation is now reversed. No one watches an ad on YouTube unless they want to, and so, your talent buy is your media buy.

This is going to amplify a different sort of creative agency as well as give recognizable talent more leverage. A good ad in the TV days was annoying but led to action. A good ad today creates enrollment and buzz. Attention is insufficient, though. Ghostbusters was seen by millions, but it didn’t sell many vintage Hearses.

[And why is this a lousy ad? I love my Rivian, but not because it has a Ghostbuster button. The first job of advertising a new brand is to earn it a position, to give us a story about what you’d like to stand for. Who it’s for and how we’re going to feel when we wear the label you’re offering us. Jaguar dropped the ball when they re-branded last year. AI companies are terrible at this as well, and it appears that Rivian missed a chance with Bill.]

Don’t cross the streams.

PS While we’re on the topic, please don’t buy cheap chocolate.

item.title: Doomberg: Jump Ball
item.description:
The source has restricted access; the returned text may be a preview.

“He hits from both sides of the plate. He’s amphibious.” – Yogi Berra

On January 6, 2025, Indonesia formally acceded to full membership in BRICS, the starts-and-stops, Russia- and China-led organization seeking to create an alternative to the US dollar-based global financial system. As the war in Iran has since made clear, whatever limitations might be plaguing America’s wildly overfunded and corrupt military-industrial complex, its economic power and broad array of financial tools are still formidable. US Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent’s economic siege has arguably been more devastating to Iran than the best efforts of Pete Hegseth’s Department of War. Through this lens, the battles over BRICS and US dollar hegemony are not just side skirmishes of World War III, but pivotal and potentially decisive confrontations.

Less than a year after Indonesia’s BRICS acceptance, student-led protests engulfed the island nation—a dubious coincidence. The campaign had many hallmarks of previous so-called color revolutions observed in former Soviet republics and other parts of the world, something Indonesian leaders seemed content to use as justification for their subsequent crackdown. Western think tanks were quick to call foul on that framing:

“ Since late August, Indonesians have been protesting against police violence and politicians’ perks. Moscow and Beijing have taken advantage of this chaos, claiming it is a direct result of the United States meddling in the domestic affairs of an Asian nation. The Indonesian government and its diplomatic partners, as well as the public, should be aware of these operations. Moreover, governments and intelligence experts should forecast the next steps Russia-China collaboration [sic] to enable preventative measures. It is not new for Russia and China to frame demonstrations as Western-engineered: they have done so in response to domestic protests in Moscow and Hong Kong. The two countries have also discredited democracy protests elsewhere—including in Ukraine, Georgia, Kazakhstan, Serbia and Thailand—using claims of covert US interference in domestic politics. ”

Organic or orchestrated? | Getty

Its accession to BRICS aside, Indonesia’s leaders have broadly tried to stay neutral in the battle between the geopolitical elephants, pursuing a strategy of strategic ambiguity. As with BRICS members India and Brazil, trade with China has created meaningful ties to that emerging superpower that would be nearly impossible to sever, yet the country still maintains significant interactions to the US military:

“ Indonesia and the United States recently elevated their decades-long military ties to a Major Defense Cooperation Partnership (MDCP), a designation that embodies the countries’ commitment to pursue advanced security measures. Under the MDCP, the nations will codevelop sophisticated asymmetric capabilities and other next-generation defense technologies across domains, and cooperate on maintenance, repair and overhaul support to ensure readiness, according to a joint statement released after Indonesian Defense Minister Sjafrie Sjamsoeddin and U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth met at the Pentagon in Washington, D.C., in April 2026. ”

A little bit for everybody | Department of War

At first blush, neutrality between superpowers would seem a near-impossible task, especially given Indonesia’s role as a gatekeeper of the Strait of Malacca, a global shipping chokepoint on par with the Strait of Hormuz in its economic significance. Surely, the country will soon be forced to firmly and decisively choose a side and cast its lot with either Washington or the Beijing-Moscow axis. Or will it? Let’s explore the strategic implications.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: The economics of agents
item.description:
From Patrick Collison:

Assorted things I’ve been mulling over regarding agents in the economy: • Companies are in some sense the original superintelligence. It’s often the case that they can use their amortized cognitive surplus to advance their interests against those of certain consumers: relative to the optimization capacity of companies, consumers can be inattentive, underinformed, irrational, etc. (Think, say, of some of the classic insurance upsells at the end of a booking process, which is typically priced substantially above what a regular policy would cost.) Herbert Simon introduced the idea of bounded rationality, and firms often end up benefiting from it. Thanks to personal agents, we will probably get somewhat more rational in how we engage with companies. • How exactly will outcomes change? Well, certain kinds of price discrimination will work less well (how do coupons work if every agent hunts fastidiously for them?), and certain kinds of customer cross-subsidy will change (today, people who forget to cancel subscriptions subsidize those who don’t). Taken across the economy as a whole, I’m not sure what the incidence of all of this will be. • In corporate strategy, people have long debated the relative importance of distribution and product quality. Perhaps you’ve made something better, but does anyone know about it? Won’t people just continue to buy the ACME Corp Mousetraps? Personal agents will, I think, act as a kind of structural subsidy for product quality. How would markets look different if individuals always spent at least 10 hours researching their purchases? On the margin, focusing on making a product better is, I think, going to become a more effective strategy for companies. This is good! • If true, a corollary is that information about product quality will become more important and impactful. Today, most people have very limited ability to aggregate and integrate such data, but agents will have insatiable thirst for such signals. (It’s often said that data is becoming more valuable because it helps in the training of models. That’s obviously true, but I think there’s a secondary way in which it’s more valuable simply as a complement to cheaper intelligence.) • A big question is whether agents will increase superstar effects (rational agents all settle on the same product) or increase dispersion (because everyone has slightly different tastes and preferences, which agents are good at eliciting, finally overcoming the artificial clustering we’ve been subjected to). • Many internet companies have monetized demand routing, which is in turn often predicated on short attention spans. “I’ll click on the first thing I see.” This has led to some amount of inefficiency, as companies try to propitiate capricious ranking algorithms and incur various placement fees. It’s not all deadweight loss (willingness to pay is itself a kind of signal, which is valuable to buyers), but it’s not great. How will the nature and value of this routing change in a world of personal agents? I don’t know the answer, but I think that the effects might be pretty big. • Much of what I’m writing hinges on the assumption that personal agents will be on the consumer’s side. I suspect that that will be the winning strategy, but whether it’s true, and what it means to be true, involves a lot of other questions. Taken as a whole, the market is a massively parallelized, decentralized, and highly imperfect value attribution machine, and, taking stock of all of the effects, it seems to me that the quality point may well be the biggest: that agents will change the nature of the backpropagation such that the rewards for better products increase. Maybe this is too optimistic, but I suspect (and hope) that companies that make things that they’re proud of will feel that the universe is a little more partisan in their favor.

In addition to those mechanisms, I might also expect some prices to be more volatile.  Suppliers will attempt to use agents to collude, and the law may not have a simple way of stopping this practice, due to illegibility.  The practice could be illegible and unintended by the merchants themselves.  But collusion of course tends not to be stable.  So (some) prices may swoon upwards for a while, and then take sudden dips as either the collusion breaks down or new entry occurs…

item.title: Marginal Revolution: California in-migration and out-migration
item.description:
Long-run U.S. population movements have been driven more by natural amenities than by jobs, and California, rich in both uniform and complementary climates, should be a persistent net gainer of domestic migrants. It has instead lost residents to other states every year since about 1990. This paper argues that its amenities are unchanged and that the location rents they generate have been captured politically. Capture through a land tax would be borne by landowners and would move no one. Capture through mobile tax bases-above all a steeply progressive income tax-and through restrictions on housing supply does move people, and moves particular people. Where the revenue also finances redistribution, high earners pay far more than the value of the services they receive, which pushes them out on a second count; the income tax also raises the pre-tax wages firms must pay, so jobs leave with households. Proposition 13 shifts capture onto mobile tax bases and locks long-tenured owners in place, so observed out-migration understates the underlying pressure. Internal Revenue Service data show that in 2022-23 California’s out-migrants outnumbered its in-migrants by 40 percent overall but by 64 percent among households with incomes of $200,000 or more, a pattern reversed in low-tax states. A simple cross-state comparison, which cannot hold production advantages constant, shows no relation between tax burdens and natural amenities, suggesting that competition among amenity-rich states limits capture; California, which taxes well beyond what its neighbors charge, loses residents disproportionately to them. Border comparisons and data on homeowners’ length of residence are consistent with the argument.

Here is more from Philiip E. Graves, via the excellent Kevin Lewis.

item.title: Futility Closet: Road Thoughts
item.description:
A puzzle by Sam Loyd:

Here is a pretty problem which I figured out during a ride from Bixley to Quixley astride a razor-back mule. I asked Don Pedro, a native guide who walked ahead of me pulling the mule forward by its reins, if my steed had another gait. He said it had but that it was much slower, so I pursued my journey at uniform speed. To encourage Don Pedro, who was my chief propelling power, I said we would pass through Pixley, so as to get some liquid refreshments; and from that moment he could think of nothing but Pixley. After we had been traveling for forty minutes I asked how far we had gone. Don Pedro replied: ‘Just half as far as it is to Pixley.’ After creeping along for seven miles more I asked: ‘How far is it to Quixley?’ He replied as before: ‘Just half as far as it is to Pixley.’ We arrived at Quixley in another hour, which induces me to ask you to determine the distance from Bixley to Quixley.

Two time intervals are given, but they’re not needed to solve the problem. The first question is asked between Bixley and Pixley; call that point x. The second question is asked between Pixley and Quixley; call that point y. The distance between x and y is 7 miles. The distance from x to Pixley is two-thirds the distance from Bixley to Pixley, and the distance from y to Pixley is two-thirds the distance between Pixley and Quixley. So the distance from x to y, 7 miles, is two-thirds the total distance, which must be 10.5 miles.

item.title: Futility Closet: The Ringelmann Effect
item.description:
In studying the relationship between productivity and efficiency in 1913, French agricultural engineer Maximilien Ringelmann found that members of a group perform worse on average as the size of the group increases. In a tug of war, as the size of a team grows, each member begins to “loaf,” relying on his teammates to put forth the necessary effort. Worse, the team’s growing size makes it increasingly difficult to coordinate its actions.

Interestingly, though, ants have been shown to increase in efficiency when working in teams. New World army ants can carry larger loads as a team than if the burden were distributed among them individually, and Weaver ants organize pulling chains that can effectively double the strength of each member. So “the Ringelmann effect” isn’t inescapable.

item.title: Marginal Revolution: The origin of risk
item.description:
From the QJE, by Alexandr Kopytov, Mathieu Taschereau-Dumouchel, and Zebang Xu:

We propose a tractable model in which risk, at both the micro and macro levels, is endogenous and driven by incentives. In the model, each firm chooses the mean and the variance of its productivity process, as well as how it covaries with the productivity of other firms. Aggregate risk arises when firms select productivity processes that are correlated with one another. The theory predicts that larger firms and those with lower markups are less volatile and less correlated with aggregate productivity. We find support for these predictions in the data. Through their impact on risk-taking decisions, distortions such as taxes and markups can make GDP more volatile in equilibrium. In a calibrated version of the model, removing distortions significantly reduces GDP volatility.

Fischer Black!  (And my own earlier book Risk and Business Cycles).  Via the excellent Kevin Lewis.

item.title: Futility Closet: Lingua Franca
item.description:
Mathematician Giuseppe Peano created an auxiliary language to facilitate communication between people of different nations. Latin already served as an international language, he reasoned; “Latino sine flexione” could retain that language’s vocabulary but simplify its grammar as much as possible. In a 1908 speech announcing the idea, he began speaking in classical Latin and adopted each simplification as he described it until he was speaking in the new language. Here’s the Lord’s Prayer:

Nostro patre, qui es in caelos, que tuo nomine fi sanctificato; que tuo regno adveni; que tuo voluntate es facto sicut in caelo et in terra. Da hodie ad nos nostro pane quotidiano, et remitte ad nos nostro debitos, sicut et nos remitte ad nostro debitores. Et non induce nos in tentatione, sed libera nos ab malo. Amen.

In the end it was not widely adopted, but most of Peano’s books and papers are written in his proposed language.

item.title: Seth's Blog: Thin friction and thicker walls
item.description:
Civilized culture is based on a thin sort of friction. You don’t yell at the library, act boorish at a restaurant or hassle a minor celebrity at the supermarket. It’s just not done.

The result of these human layers and inferences are cues and norms that add up to a connected, generative society.

Add selfish hustle, AI agents and cheap bots, and the thin friction is insufficient. They can multiply exponentially, care little about being shunned and have no interest in their reputation.

Fake sincerity is now cheap. Interchangeable identities subvert a generations-long tradition of owning your words and your actions.

You’ll miss the thin friction when it’s gone, replaced by taller, thicker walls. You might already be noticing it.

Interactivity and permeability to those we don’t know well were largely overlooked foundations in the creation of learning, science and culture. We figured out a scalable approach to “knock knock, who’s there” but now it’s going away.

You won’t be able to knock unless you’re invited first. Of course, the invitation will probably be filtered out.
